title: Santeria and the roots of Cuban music
summary: He says the Yoruba religion was to them like any church, and from its rhythms came mambo, salsa and cha-cha-cha.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Okay. These jam sessions, the only thing I can think of calling them, they were African in origin, right? Were they taken from any religious cults? - the music - they used the sacred bata drum?

Well, let me tell you. Ah - to us - the Yoruba religion o Santeria o brujeria, whatever they call it, to us was like the Catholic religion or Protestant or Pentecostal or whatever. We create, we made an extract, we extract ours all those rhythms and we created what is the Cuban music now, what is Salsa, Mambo, Chachacha, Columbia, whatever.
So what you are saying then, from these religious cult music is where the Afro-Cuban, the Afro-Cuban root music came?
